Triggers.value: Similar weather conditions to when the event happened

Maladaptive Strategies.value: avoid relaxing because it feels dangerous
try hard not think about the trauma

Memory.value: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once
I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.
My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.

issues.explanation: For a natural disaster trauma, the trigger set is hard to reconcile with the trauma type and with the rest of the profile. Motorcycle noise, ambulances, and hospital/antiseptic smells together suggest an injury/medical-emergency aftermath pattern rather than a primary disaster-linked cue pattern. A disaster survivor could have some of these cues, but all three together without any disaster-specific trigger makes the trigger node clinically questionable.

'Guilt on recall' is not impossible after a natural disaster, but in this profile it lacks support from any negative appraisal items and sits awkwardly alongside a formulation where Memory is strongly linked to Triggers and Maladaptive Strategies but not to Negative Appraisals or Threat. The selected memory items otherwise describe sensory reliving and fragmented snapshots; adding intense guilt introduces a meaning-based response not reflected elsewhere.

issues.item: Triggers: Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell
issues.explanation: 'Wear concealing clothing to avoid being noticed' is difficult to connect to the listed triggers and memory items for a natural disaster survivor. It implies fears about being seen, targeted, or scrutinized, which are not represented in the trigger or memory content and are not supported by active edges involving threat or negative appraisals.

issues.item: Concealing Clothing: wear concealing clothing to avoid being noticed
issues.explanation: For a natural disaster trauma, 'wear concealing clothing to avoid being noticed' is hard to reconcile with the presented trigger pattern and memory content. This strategy implies interpersonal scrutiny or targeted threat, but the profile contains no corresponding threat/appraisal items and the trauma type is non-interpersonal.

issues.item: Body Monitoring: constantly check body for signs of danger or injury
issues.explanation: 'Constantly check body for signs of danger or injury' is weakly grounded in the rest of the profile. The triggers are external reminder cues and the memory items emphasize sensory reliving/snapshot recall, but there is no corresponding bodily injury theme, threat belief, or appraisal that would make persistent body checking a coherent central strategy.

issues.item: Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt
issues.explanation: 'When I remember the event I feel intense guilt' is not impossible after a natural disaster, but in this profile it lacks support from any negative appraisal content and does not fit the otherwise cue-driven sensory reliving formulation. It stands out as an unsupported meaning-based reaction within a profile whose active edges are concentrated around triggers, memory, and maladaptive strategies rather than appraisals.

issues.item: Concealing Clothing: wear concealing clothing to avoid being noticed
issues.explanation: This item is not clinically well aligned with the rest of the profile for a natural-disaster trauma. The triggers and memory items consistently describe sensory re-experiencing of a disaster, and the formulation strongly links Triggers ↔ Memory ↔ Maladaptive Strategies. 'Concealing clothing to avoid being noticed' implies an interpersonal scrutiny or targeted-harm concern that is not supported by the listed triggers, memory content, or any threat/appraisal items. It addresses a different problem type than the rest of the profile and is hard to explain as part of the same PTSD presentation.

vignette:
Kiet Phanomvan is a thirty-one-year-old Cambodian-American judge who has been married for three years and, until recently, was regarded by colleagues as one of the most composed and methodical members of the bench. He presented for psychological assessment approximately eight months after surviving a catastrophic flash flood that struck his coastal hometown during what had begun as an unremarkable autumn afternoon. The sky that day had been a particular shade of bruised grey, the air carrying the thick, mineral weight that precedes serious rain, and within two hours the streets had become channels of brown water moving with the force and indifference of something alive. Kiet was trapped for nearly six hours on the second floor of a community building, watching through a window as vehicles were carried past and listening to voices that eventually went silent. When emergency services finally reached him, he was transported by ambulance through streets still partially submerged, the interior of the vehicle saturated with the sharp antiseptic smell of medical supplies pressed against his face. He was physically unharmed. He told the intake clinician he had not expected that to matter as much as it apparently does.

In the weeks that followed, Kiet found that certain sensory details had lodged themselves in his mind not as a continuous narrative but as a series of discrete, frozen images - the waterline creeping up the exterior wall, a child's shoe turning slowly in the current below, the particular angle of light through a cracked window. Each image was vivid and complete in itself, and when one surfaced it brought with it no before or after, only the moment, rendered in full sensory detail. He described the experience as being pulled without warning back into the room - not remembering it, but inhabiting it again, the cold and the smell and the sound of the water entirely present. These intrusions were not frequent in the early weeks, but they were total when they came.

The triggers that reliably activated these episodes became apparent to Kiet before he had the language to name what was happening. The sound of an ambulance siren - a sound he encountered with some regularity given that the courthouse sat two blocks from a major hospital - would stop him mid-sentence during proceedings and send a current of alarm through his chest that he struggled to conceal from counsel and defendants. The antiseptic smell that clung to the hospital corridor he sometimes passed during lunch became something he began routing his walk to avoid. Most reliably of all, overcast skies carrying that particular grey-green quality would produce, within minutes, a vivid intrusion of the flood's earliest moments. On those days the memories arrived with a force that felt less like recollection and more like ambush, and Kiet found himself scanning the courtroom windows with an attention that had nothing to do with the case before him.

It was the intrusions themselves - their completeness, their insistence - that drove the strategies Kiet constructed to manage his days. He had come to believe that if he could keep his mind occupied and vigilant at all times, he could prevent the memories from finding purchase. He worked to suppress any thought that drifted toward the flood, redirecting his attention with a concentration that left him exhausted by evening. He had stopped going out beyond what his professional obligations required, reasoning that exposure to unpredictable sensory environments - a passing ambulance, a change in weather, the wrong smell in a corridor - was simply an unnecessary risk. He had also stopped allowing himself to rest. Relaxation, he had concluded, felt genuinely dangerous, as though lowering his guard was the condition the memories were waiting for. He had not sat in the garden with his wife since the summer. She had stopped suggesting it. The avoidance had its own logic, and for a time it seemed to hold. But the strategies themselves had begun to reshape his environment: the routes he took, the windows he avoided, the silences he kept at home all constituted a landscape that kept the flood perpetually near, its absence a form of presence, so that the very effort of not-remembering became the thing that kept the triggers close.

Kiet sought help after missing a day on the bench for the first time in his career - a morning when the sky turned the wrong colour and he could not make himself leave the house. What he most feared, he said quietly, was that this was now simply who he was. What he most hoped was that it wasn't.
